families.context_notes:
FACT-CHECK SUMMARY (2026-10-09): I re-fetched every cited URL live; none were taken from cache.
- Henriksen et al. 2023 PDF: downloaded from sservi.directus.app (HTTP 200, MD5 identical to the earlier cached copy). It is the 2023 European Lunar Symposium abstract book; the abstract is on PDF pp. 134-135. I rendered Table 1 myself with PyMuPDF to confirm each paired cell and the minus signs.
- LROC RDR pages: all 12 re-fetched live from data.lroc.im-ldi.com. Every center and bound quoted in the input matched. The product-name suffixes (e.g. P836S2912) encode the same centers.
- IAU Gazetteer: verified for Slater, Mons Mouton, Cabeus B, de Gerlache, Haworth, Malapert, Nobile and Amundsen. The listed system is "Planetographic, +East, -180..180", which for the spherical Moon reference equals planetocentric.
No site was dropped; every coordinate is stated in at least one primary source.

CORRECTIONS MADE:
(a) The input attributed the distances "about 125 miles" (Peak near Cabeus B) and "about 31 mi" (de Gerlache Rim 2) to NASA. They come from Astronomy.com; NASA's Oct 2024 release gives no distances or coordinates.
(b) The Nobile Rim 1 source NAC_ROI_MTMOUTONLOB is the 95-105 deg sub-solar sub-mosaic B, not the combined mosaic. I replaced it with NAC_ROI_MTMOUTONLO1.
(c) de Gerlache Rim 1 is 17.4 km from the crater center, not 16 km. The Malapert table-vs-LROC offset is 1.3 km, not about 1 km.
(d) Added Wikipedia's statement that Mons Mouton was "previously sometimes referred to as Leibnitz Beta". This independently supports the 2022 Leibnitz Beta Plateau to 2024 Mons Mouton mapping; NASA itself never states the rename.
(e) Added the Gazetteer link for Nobile (Feature/4321) and two independent consistency points for Connecting Ridge.

KEY CAVEAT (not independent): Henriksen Table 1 "centers" are the midpoints of the corresponding LROC mosaic lat/lon extents. For example, Haworth: (-87.39 + -86.11)/2 = -86.75 and (-34.98 + -12.36)/2 = -23.67; the same holds for Malapert, Nobile Rim 2, Amundsen, Faustini, Peak near Shackleton and de Gerlache-Kocher. So the Table 1 and LROC values come from one LROC/ASU team, and their agreement is not independent confirmation. They are bounding-box centers of mosaics built to cover NASA's regions, not NASA-published centers. NASA's 2022 release says each region is about 15x15 km and lies within 6 deg of the pole. Nobile Rim 2's center is at 6.05 deg, which is marginal.

REGION LIST STATUS (confirmed live):
- Aug 19 2022, 13 regions: Faustini Rim A, Peak Near Shackleton, Connecting Ridge, Connecting Ridge Extension, de Gerlache Rim 1, de Gerlache Rim 2, de Gerlache-Kocher Massif, Haworth, Malapert Massif, Leibnitz Beta Plateau, Nobile Rim 1, Nobile Rim 2, Amundsen Rim. https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-identifies-candidate-regions-for-landing-next-americans-on-Moon/
- Oct 28 2024 (RELEASE 24-136), 9 regions: Peak near Cabeus B, Haworth, Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton Plateau, Mons Mouton, Nobile Rim 1, Nobile Rim 2, de Gerlache Rim 2, Slater Plain. https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-provides-update-on-artemis-iii-moon-landing-regions/
- Comparing the lists (my inference): 6 retained, with Mons Mouton = Leibnitz Beta Plateau; 3 added (Peak near Cabeus B, Mons Mouton Plateau, Slater Plain); 7 dropped.
- George, Rubio, Lawrence & Curell, LPSC 2026 #1901 (https://www.hou.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2026/pdf/1901.pdf), fetched live, repeats the same 9 regions with no coordinates. It says removed regions are not unsuitable and that the refinement "does not affect site selection for Artemis IV and later missions".
- No official change to the 9-region list was found for 2025-2026.

MISSION STATUS (verified via news):
- On 27 Feb 2026 Administrator Isaacman made Artemis III a low-Earth-orbit rendezvous and docking test with the HLS landers, targeted for late 2027. The first landing moved to Artemis IV, targeted for early 2028.
- The Artemis III crew was named on 9 Jun 2026: Bresnik, Parmitano (ESA), Rubio, Douglas.
- NASA's Artemis IV page (updated 16 Mar 2026, fetched live) says the agency "has identified nine candidate landing regions near the lunar South Pole".
- SpacePolicyOnline (16 Mar 2026): Associate Administrator Kshatriya said early-landing specifications have been "opened up" but NASA is "not yet giving up on the South Pole". Artemis II pilot Victor Glover publicly suggested not going to the south pole first. Treat the 9 regions as current but subject to change.

GAPS:
- Slater Plain: no numeric center exists in any accessible source, so I give only the Slater crater locator.
- Wueller et al. 2026, JGR Planets (doi:10.1029/2025JE009434; CC-BY; reports 130 candidate landing sites inside the Artemis regions) could not be read. Wiley returned 403. The ZORA repository copy sits behind a bot-check page, which I did not bypass. The ETH Research Collection copy returned HTTP 429 (rate limited). It may hold numeric site coordinates, including for Slater Plain, if retrieved manually.

CONVENTIONS: Longitudes are east-positive in -180..180. LROC center longitudes on a 0-360 scale were converted: 291.2 -> -68.8, 293.3 -> -66.7, 336.3 -> -23.7, 243.6 -> -116.4; LROC min/max bounds are already in -180..180. Gracy & Lee 209.94767 E -> -150.05 E. Martin et al. 222.1 E -> -137.9 E.

families.context_notes:
Fact-check summary (2026-10-09). No sites were dropped: every coordinate was found stated in at least one source. Changes made: (1) The six Bussey 2010 points (A, B, C, D, M1, M2) were downgraded from medium to low confidence. Their numbers appear only in the Wikipedia table that cites the paper; I checked both the rendered page and the raw wikitext. The Icarus paper is closed access (Crossref and OpenAlex have no abstract), and no independent restatement turned up in Bussey's EGU2011 and EPSC2012/2013 abstracts or in Elvis et al. 2016. The points are geographically consistent with the De Rosa RoIs, within 0.4-1.8 km. (2) The eight LROC low-Sun mosaic centers were reclassified from high-illumination-point to artemis-iii-region, because LROC describes each product as a mosaic of an Artemis III candidate site, not an illumination point. The orchestrator may need to deduplicate them against an artemis-iii-region list. (3) The LROC ridge/rim intersection (89.684°S, 196.739°E) was reclassified to crater-or-massif-feature because it is a geomorphic location. (4) Fixed the GR1 what_it_says typo, corrected the de Gerlache 'original' network label (it is 'UNKNOWN'), and removed the unverified VIPER wording from the Mons Mouton entry.

How I verified: I downloaded the PDFs and extracted text with pdftotext. Sources were De Rosa 2012 arXiv:1208.5587 Table 2, Gläser 2018 NTRS accepted manuscript Tables 1-2 (PSS 162, doi:10.1016/j.pss.2017.07.006), the EPSC2014-136 spot table, and the Barker 2021 NTRS manuscript. Every number matched the input exactly. I also recomputed the De Rosa stereographic X/Y from lat/lon (R = 1737.4 km, lon 0 up, 90°E right). It reproduces all 12 rows within rounding, which confirms east-positive longitude and spherical (planetocentric) latitude. I parsed the USGS gazetteer HTML per control-network block; all LOLA 2011 values match. I re-fetched all LROC RDR pages, which state '360 positive east', and the LROC featured and exhibit pages and NASA SVS 4075; all match. Barker 2021 confirms that Sites 1, 4, 7 and 11 (Mazarico 2011 Table 3 numbering) correspond to De Rosa CR1, SR1, SV1 and GR1, that Sites 1 and 4 correspond to Gläser 2018 C1 and S, and that Site 8 = SR2. PGDA product 78 confirms Site42 = de Gerlache-Kocher massif, DM2 = Nobile rim 2 and LM7 = Faustini Rim A, but it publishes no lat/lon. The Mazarico 2011 and Speyerer & Robinson 2013 points are secondary, taken from Gläser 2018 Table 1, whose co-authors include Mazarico, Speyerer and Robinson. The originals could not be read (NTRS 20120010094 has no download), so those entries stay at medium.

Conventions: all longitudes are east-positive in -180..180. Gläser and the LROC RDRs use 0-360°E; Wikipedia's Bussey table uses W/E. De Rosa gives coordinates in the ME/PA DE421 frame, and LOLA products use MOON_ME DE421; the difference from the app's DE440 MOON_ME is negligible at this precision. The gazetteer labels its values 'Planetographic', which equals planetocentric for the spherical lunar reference.

Artemis status, verified on NASA pages: 13 regions were announced on 19 Aug 2022. On 28 Oct 2024 NASA named nine: Peak near Cabeus B, Haworth, Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton Plateau, Mons Mouton, Nobile Rim 1, Nobile Rim 2, de Gerlache Rim 2 and Slater Plain. George et al., LPSC 2026 (NTRS 20250011660) confirms the same nine. Not carried over from 2022 were Faustini Rim A, Peak Near Shackleton, Connecting Ridge, Connecting Ridge Extension, de Gerlache Rim 1, de Gerlache-Kocher Massif and Amundsen Rim. Leibnitz Beta Plateau was effectively superseded by the Mons Mouton regions after the 2022 IAU renaming. A NASA release of 9 Jun 2026 ('NASA Marches Toward Artemis III Mission in 2027, Names Crew Members') says Artemis III will run tests in Earth orbit in 2027, including rendezvous and docking with HLS test articles, and that Artemis IV is the first planned crewed South Pole landing, in 2028. That claim, which the input sourced only from news reports, is now confirmed by NASA.

Fact-check pass, 2026-10-08/09. Of the 10 input sites, all 10 are kept and no coordinate values changed. These corrections were made:

(d) Chang'e-7: confidence stays low. The only numeric source is a Weibo post cited by Wikipedia. By my calculation the point is about 15 km outside Shackleton's rim, on a local high.
(e) LUPEX: confidence stays low. It is secondhand ('could be'), but an ISRO SAC LPSC 2024 abstract (#1898) independently places the proposed LUPEX site on the same Shackleton-de Gerlache ridge, with an OHRC image centred at 89.2836°S, 140.556°W.

Conventions: the IAU Gazetteer gives 'Planetographic +East -180..180', which is effectively planetocentric for the spherical Moon. LROC, Beyer et al. and NSSDC use east-positive longitude. Marshall et al. use Mean Earth selenocentric coordinates.
